newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. mixed signals leave doubts over Iraq policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mixed signals leave doubts over Iraq policy.

text.p: The United States has been sending mixed signals that have left a question mark over its next move in its high-stakes standoff with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

Will Washington attack its Gulf War foe again, or will the world's only superpower sit back and watch how the unpredictable Iraqi leader responds to a continuing U.S. military buildup in the oil-rich region?
Senior U.S. officials at home and in the Gulf gave contradictory signals, raising doubts about further U.S. attacks even as they concentrate more forces in the region.

Some Gulf Arab officials see the lack of U.S. clarity as a curse that makes it harder to coordinate policy and restore the 1991 Gulf War alliance against Iraq. They recall the ambiguity in Washington's Iraq policy in 1990 that some historians say encouraged Saddam to invade Kuwait on August 2 of that year.
But some Western officials see the ambiguity as a blessing that in the post-Gulf War political world will keep Saddam off balance and cautious.
"A little bit of ambiguity could be a good thing," a senior diplomat said. "It deprives him of the initiative."
"But Saddam does need to know one thing for sure -- that if he continues to play this cat and mouse game with the Gulf, it will come with a price."

Diplomats said a weekend tour of three Gulf Arab states by U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry produced more questions than answers about what Washington wants in the region, other than the general goal of a united front against Kuwait's unrepentant neighbour.

On a visit to Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, Perry said on Sunday a strike at Iraq was still possible but Washington's U.N. envoy Madeleine Albright said she did not expect further attacks on Iraq or further defiance of no-fly zones by Saddam.
Some diplomats reacted with dismay to the mixed signals.

"There seems to be no American consensus on what to do and where they want to go. The result is that they have less and less people following them. They are acting as if they are the boss in the region," said a Western diplomat in Kuwait.
"The suspicion has arisen that they do not know what they want and do not have a clear long-term vision for the region."

The latest crisis between the United States and Iraq started at the beginning of the month when Iraq intervened in factional fighting in its Kurdish north, an area closed to its forces by the West for the past five years.
Washington retaliated by firing 44 cruise missiles at air defences in southern Iraq. It also expanded a southern Iraq no-fly zone, closed to Iraqi planes but patrolled by western powers.
Iraq rejected the no-fly zone and fired six missiles at U.S. planes in the zone last week. But, as U.S. retaliation neared, Iraq reversed course on Friday and said it would not attack air patrols.

Most regional allies gave no support to the U.S. action and were unwilling to help Washington's buildup of ships and warplanes. Even Kuwait, the only Arab state to openly back the earlier U.S. missile strikes, did not formally agree to the presence of extra U.S. ground troops until Monday.
Diplomats said Perry did not spell out in the Gulf exactly what Iraq must do to avoid further strikes, concentrating on overall policy towards Baghdad.
Western sources said they could not confirm reports Perry said Baghdad had to remove all air defence missiles from the southern no-fly zone or face new strikes.
Even if he made the demand, it may have left open exactly how and when Iraq would have to dismantle the stragically important defences.
The main remaining air defences in the southern no-fly zone are in a dense network of fixed and mobile installations south of Baghdad between the 32nd and 33rd parallels -- the expanded no-fly zone.
"Perhaps he would have to drive out the mobile sites while removing the missiles from the fixed sites," a diplomat said.
"With satellite imaging it should be possible to verify the withdrawals. But perhaps Washington only wants him to withdraw the crews and switch off the machinery. No one seems to know."
